lesson.title: The Candidates Test: Why Absolute Extrema Can Only Hide in Two Places
lesson.summary: On a closed interval, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees a function has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum, and the Candidates Test narrows the entire search down to just two kinds of locations: critical numbers inside the interval, or the two endpoints.
lesson.body:
If f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that f actually attains an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value somewhere on [a, b]. That existence guarantee matters: without it, searching for a global maximum could be a search for something that does not exist. With it settled, the only remaining question is where to look.

Suppose the absolute maximum happens at some point c strictly inside the interval, meaning a is less than c and c is less than b. Since f(c) is at least as large as every other value of f on the whole interval, it is certainly at least as large as every value nearby, so c is automatically a local maximum too. If f is differentiable at c, Fermat's theorem on interior extrema then forces f'(c) = 0. If f is not differentiable at c, that failure of differentiability makes c a critical number by definition anyway. Either way, an absolute extremum sitting at an interior point must be a critical number. The only other possibility left is that the absolute extremum sits at one of the two endpoints, a or b, where the interior argument does not apply since there is no room on one side to compare against. Put together, these two cases are the entire Candidates Test: an absolute maximum or minimum on [a, b] can only occur at a critical number inside (a, b), or at an endpoint.

Consider f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 on the closed interval [-1, 3]. Differentiating gives f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2), so the critical numbers are x = 0 and x = 2, both comfortably inside (-1, 3). The full candidate list is therefore x = -1, x = 0, x = 2, and x = 3, two endpoints and two interior critical numbers. Evaluating f at each: f(-1) = -1 - 3 = -4, f(0) = 0, f(2) = 8 - 12 = -4, and f(3) = 27 - 27 = 0. Comparing these four numbers, the largest value is 0, reached at both x = 0 and x = 3, so that is the absolute maximum, and the smallest value is -4, reached at both x = -1 and x = 2, so that is the absolute minimum. Notice the theorem never said the extrema had to be unique. The next section turns this exact reasoning into a clean, repeatable algorithm called the Closed Interval Method.
